artifacts.title: TRT and fertility what to ask
artifacts.intro: Raise fertility before you start, because testosterone therapy suppresses the body's own testosterone production, and with it sperm production — this is an expected effect of the treatment rather than an unusual side effect. If you may want children, that conversation changes what you are offered: there are alternative approaches intended to raise testosterone without the same suppression, and there is the option of banking sperm beforehand. Recovery after stopping varies between individuals and is not guaranteed, which is precisely why the discussion belongs before the first prescription.

artifacts.title: Why this conversation has to come first
artifacts.intro: The sequence matters more here than in most treatment decisions.
items: Suppression of sperm production is an expected consequence of testosterone therapy, not a rare complication.
A baseline semen analysis is only a baseline if it is taken before treatment starts.
Alternatives intended to preserve fertility are easiest to consider before a prescription is written.
Sperm banking is straightforward beforehand and more complicated afterwards.
Recovery after stopping varies between individuals, so it cannot be relied on as the plan.
If a clinic does not raise fertility during your evaluation, raise it yourself — and treat the omission as information about the clinic.

artifacts.title: Online TRT vs local clinic which is safer
artifacts.intro: Neither format is inherently safer — the safeguards are. A telehealth clinic that requires morning blood testing, confirms an out-of-range result before prescribing, schedules follow-up labs, and names its prescribing clinician is safer than a local clinic that does none of those. Judge the specific practice on testing, monitoring, prescriber identity, and how it handles an abnormal result, and treat 'online' or 'local' as a logistics question rather than a safety verdict.

artifacts.title: Safeguards that matter more than the format
artifacts.intro: This is decision-support for talking to a clinician. It is not medical advice, and it does not replace evaluation by a licensed physician who knows your history.
items: A morning blood test, drawn before treatment, is the starting point for any legitimate evaluation.
A single out-of-range result should be confirmed with a repeat before a prescription follows.

Symptoms that overlap with low testosterone — fatigue, low mood, poor sleep, low libido — also belong to sleep apnoea, thyroid disease, anaemia, and depression. A clinic that never considers those is not evaluating you.
Monitoring after starting matters as much as the decision to start.
Testosterone is a controlled substance in the United States; a clinic casual about prescribing is a signal in itself.
Bring your own physician into the loop regardless of which format you choose.

artifacts.title: TRT side effects what to watch for
artifacts.intro: The effects worth actively monitoring are the ones caught by blood work rather than by how you feel — a rising red blood cell count in particular is a recognised effect of testosterone therapy and is the main reason follow-up labs are scheduled. Alongside that, watch for worsening sleep-disordered breathing, acne or oily skin, breast tenderness, mood or sleep changes, and swelling. Fertility suppression is expected rather than a side effect to watch for. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or leg swelling needs urgent medical assessment, not a message to the clinic.

artifacts.title: How do I verify a TRT clinic's credentials and licensing
artifacts.intro: Verify three things independently of the clinic's own website: the prescribing clinician's licence through the state medical board, the dispensing pharmacy through the state board of pharmacy, and any claimed board certification through the certifying board's own directory. A clinic that will not name its prescribing clinician cannot be verified at all, and that refusal is the finding. Do this before you pay, because every one of these checks is free and takes minutes.

artifacts.title: How to run the checks
artifacts.intro: Fifteen minutes, before you pay anything.
items: Search for the state medical board of the state you live in — use the board's own site, not a directory that aggregates it.
Search the clinician's name in the licence lookup. Confirm the licence is active and note the type.
Read any disciplinary record shown, and compare it with what the clinic disclosed.
For a claimed board certification, look the clinician up in that board's own directory.
Search your state board of pharmacy for the dispensing pharmacy.
Save screenshots of what you verified, with the date.
If any check fails or cannot be completed, ask the clinic directly and treat a non-answer as a negative.

artifacts.title: How to compare TRT clinics in 2026
artifacts.intro: Compare TRT clinics on four things that are verifiable before you pay: who prescribes and what their credentials are, what baseline testing is required before a prescription is issued, how monitoring is scheduled afterwards, and what the total cost is including labs. Telehealth clinics vary most on the first two — a clinic that will prescribe without a baseline blood panel and a documented clinical assessment is the clearest disqualifier. Ask every clinic the same set of questions and compare the answers side by side.

artifacts.title: What questions should I ask a TRT clinic at the first consultation
artifacts.intro: Ask for the twelve-month total, not the monthly price. TRT is billed in four separate streams — the consultation, the medication, the laboratory work, and any ongoing membership or subscription fee — and headline pricing usually covers only one or two of them. Labs are the line most often excluded and the one that recurs. At a first consultation, ask what each stream costs, what is included, what your insurance may cover, and what happens to the price if your dose or formulation changes.
